hypothesis: The mixdown is not a constant-gain linear sum of the pads

hypothesis: The +/-5 dB high-frequency deviation claimed for pads 1 and 2 is a property of the model, not of which part of the sequence a take happened to capture
test: Capture pad 2 twice and compare the two takes band by band; the same pad must reproduce within ~1 dB for the claim to stand
notes: sparse percussive pads are the case where take coverage could distort the average spectrum

hypothesis: The high-frequency excess on pads 1 and 2 comes from our master-bus model: with the compressor bypassed the model's band shape matches the capture and the +5 dB disappears
test: Render pad 2 with and without master.apply_to_stems and compare each band shape against the capture
notes: the bus is the last stage before the sum, and it is the only processing left after the one-shot path was proved faithful

hypothesis: A single device hit of pad 2 differs in spectrum from our rendered hit; comparing only the first hit (before tap drift accumulates) will show the same high-frequency excess
test: Extract the first onset of the pad-2 capture and the matching model hit, align them on a 200 ms window, and compare octave-band shapes
notes: Single-hit comparison keeps the +7.8 dB tilt at 14.5 kHz, so it is per-hit content, not hit count. Decay is not the cause either: fitting EnvelopeScales.decay jointly over pads 0/1/2/9 gives a mean band spread 4.44 dB at decay=0 and 5.75-7.14 dB with any decay. Also found that RenderParams.decay_scale_s and attack_scale_s are declared but never read (dead parameters)

hypothesis: The device applies a global high-frequency shelf that the converter does not model, so adding it should lower the mixdown residual as well as the per-pad tilt
test: Sweep a post-bus high shelf (0..+8 dB above a sweepable corner) and measure the model residual against the reference mixdown
notes: Every shelf tried made the mixdown worse: +1 dB @8k -> 0.18138, +2 -> 0.18171, +3 -> 0.18213, and steeper at lower corners. No global high-frequency stage is missing

hypothesis: The +5..+8 dB high-frequency deviation seen on pads 1 and 2 is audible-band content that the converter gets wrong
test: Put the deviation in absolute terms: compare the device hit and the raw sample band by band in dBFS, not in relative dB
notes: Device hit is ~17 dB below the sample at the tap's routing gain; the 14.5 kHz band sits at -85.2 dBFS against a -17.1 dBFS hit peak, i.e. 68 dB down. The +7.5 dB 'excess' is a ratio between two near-noise bands. It cannot matter to the mixdown, and modelling it would add noise. Ignore

hypothesis: The remaining residual is a timing error: some pads should be shifted by a fraction of a millisecond
test: Sweep a fractional per-pad delay (-4..+4 ms) against the mixdown, one pad at a time
notes: Only pad 16 moves the residual at all (-0.2 ms, -0.0019); every other pad's optimum is 0.0 ms. Timing is not the residual

hypothesis: A global gain error accounts for a large part of the residual
test: Sweep a global output gain -6..+6 dB against the mixdown
notes: Optimum +0.5 dB gives 0.17992 against 0.18112: 0.5 dB, not dB

hypothesis: The master chain has stages we never modelled
test: Dump every insert on every track of the project
notes: Outputs 1/2 carries three ENABLED inserts: Pad-Controlled FXs, Flex Beat Player, Color Compressor; Submix 1 carries an LP Filter. Only the Color Compressor is modelled. They appear to be idle in this project (correlation 0.94), but they are unmodelled and self-declared as such by the audit

hypothesis: The -21 dB deficit of pad 10 comes from the warped-pad gate being far too aggressive
test: Render pad 10 with and without gate, calibrate the tap gain from the bass, compare RMS
notes: gate=warped gives pad 10 as 21.6 dB TOO QUIET; gate=none is 9.3 dB too loud. The gate over-attenuates by 31 dB. Removing it raises the mixdown residual to 0.20127, so the gate is reducing the metric, not the error

hypothesis: Per-pad level errors measured from the captures can be corrected with a volume mapping gain = volume^2
test: Rewrite every pad volume as volume^2 and measure the mixdown
notes: residual 0.19364 (worse) although correlation rises to 0.9422->0.9435 at exponent 1.5. The capture-based level calibration contradicts the mixdown, so it is not trustworthy enough to ship

hypothesis: Dense percussive pads are too loud because our renderer does not actually enforce monophony, so overlapping one-shots sum
test: Render pads 0/1/2/10 with monophonic True and False and compare RMS
notes: Pads 0/1/2 are bit-identical either way (+0.00 dB) because there are no overlaps at all: the hat's notes are 22050 samples apart (0.5 s) against a 7772-frame sample. Only pad 10 changes (-6.02 dB). Monophony is not the cause

hypothesis: Per-pad level errors measured against the firmware exports identify which stems are wrong
test: Compare every dry stem with its firmware export, tap gain anchored on the median, then compare gated and ungated
notes: Shipped: pad 10 -20.7 dB (gate), 27 -8.6, 20 -5.3, 13 -3.3, and 1 +7.8, 14 +10.2, 2 +5.5. With the gate off the warped pads move to +11.0/-0.7/+10.3/+1.0/+1.4, i.e. the gate and the warp level are separate errors that partly cancel through different pads

hypothesis: Correcting each pad to its measured level should lower the mixdown residual
test: Apply 10^(-err/20) per pad from the capture measurements, gate on and off, and measure the mixdown
notes: 0.18112 -> 0.19370 (gate on) and 0.20127 -> 0.20265 (gate off). The captures and the mixdown disagree about level, so the shipped 0.1811 is partly balanced by compensating level errors rather than by correct stems

hypothesis: The pad filter's cutoff is quadratic in Hz, (1-cutoff)^2*19960+40, not logarithmic as we model
test: Decompile DrumPadLowpassFilter<2> with Kuna, read the coefficient routine, then render every engaged pad under both cutoff laws and compare band shape to its capture
notes: Quadratic loses on 4 of 5 pads (13: 15.80 vs 10.56 dB, 16: 9.66 vs 5.67, 17: 19.84 vs 6.88, 20: 6.05 vs 4.08, 27: tie). The decompiled routine's input is not the pad cutoff; the logarithmic law is now validated against firmware audio

hypothesis: The pad filter kernel is a biquad cascade, as we model
test: Decompile the kernel at 0x247b000 and the coefficient routine
notes: The kernel is two cascaded one-pole sections with a smoothed coefficient and per-channel state, not a biquad. Our biquads approximate the response but not the topology

hypothesis: The pad filter is a Chamberlin state-variable filter whose type selects the output tap, not a biquad bank
test: Resolve FilterBlock by RTTI, decompile its processor at 0x274e720 with Kuna, then implement the recurrence and measure against the mixdown and the engaged-pad captures
notes: The processor is low+=f*band; high=x-low-qd*band; band+=f*high with a ramped f/qd and a callback choosing the tap. Implementing it wins 4 of 5 engaged pads (30.33 vs 30.60 dB total spread) and takes the mixdown from 0.178394 to 0.1783822583503335
